title: The city falls (2 Kings 25)
hookLine: Babylon burns the Temple and exile begins

cards: The last page of Kings is a hard one. These books began with Joshua crossing the Jordan into the land.
Since then the path has walked through judges and kings, a shepherd boy with a sling, a temple built by Solomon, a kingdom split in two, prophets on mountaintops, and the north carried away.
Again and again the story has come back to the land, with Jerusalem growing at the center. Now the Former Prophets end.

teach.b: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, comes with his whole army and lays siege to Jerusalem. The famine grows until there is no bread for the people of the land. The wall is broken through.
King Zedekiah flees by night and is caught in the plains of Jericho; what is done to him and his sons is told in one brutal verse, and this lesson won't linger there.

teach.h: HE BURNT THE HOUSE OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, "burnt the house of the LORD, and the king's house; and all the houses of Jerusalem". The walls are torn down.
The bronze pillars of the Temple are broken up and carried off as metal. The people are taken into exile, and only the poorest are left to tend the vines and fields.
One line sums it up: "So Judah was carried away captive out of his land." The last verses add something small.

teach.h: A CAPTIVE KING AT A TABLE.
teach.b: Years later, in Babylon, a new king lets Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, out of prison. He speaks kindly to him and gives him a seat at his table, and Jehoiachin eats bread before him for the rest of his life.
The book doesn't end on fire. It ends on a captive at a table. Jewish tradition calls the destruction the churban, and Jews mourn it on the fast of Tisha B'Av, sitting low and reading Lamentations.
Psalm 137 remembers the exiles: "By the rivers of Babylon, There we sat down, yea, we wept, When we remembered Zion." They sat down. They remembered.
That's where the next part of the story starts.

how: Jews mourn the destruction of the Temple on the fast of Tisha B'Av, when Lamentations is read in the synagogue, often while people sit on the floor or on low seats.

o: the fast day of mourning held every summer
the exiles' return from Babylon to rebuild
destruction: the fall of Jerusalem and its Temple

games.q: you're writing the last page of Kings. the city has burned and the people are in exile. how do you end the book?
o: on a list of what was lost.
on an exiled king freed and fed at a table.
games.why: the book ends with Jehoiachin out of prison, spoken to kindly, eating bread at the king of Babylon's table.

practice: Sit low, if you like, the way mourners do, and let one loss come to mind, your own or one you carry for others: a person, a home, a place that no longer exists, a community scattered.

Don't hurry to the silver lining; just sit, the way the exiles sat by the river, and remember, coming back to your breath if it gets too heavy. If you pray, you can bring the loss before God without words.

wordCard.voice: Churban. Hebrew for destruction: Babylon burns the house of the Lord and carries Judah into exile, and the book of Kings closes. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: destruction, the word Jewish tradition uses for the fall of the Temple.

carryVoice: Your line: the city fell. And the book still closes on a captive given bread. Day seven hundred eighty-one counts.
